newsitem.title: UK: Labour says London may lose services in tube sale.
newsitem.headline: Labour says London may lose services in tube sale.

text.p: The opposition Labour Party on Tuesday listed 40 London Underground stations it says are threatened by the government's plans to privatise the ailing network.
Labour's transport spokeswoman for London, Glenda Jackson, accused the ruling Conservative Party of "giving up on the concept of public transport".

"If the Tories get their way, the images of fat cat controllers lapping up the cream, whilst commuters face endless delays and cancellations, will become as much as part of the tube as they are now a part of our railways," she said, referring to the national train network which was sold last year.
The proposal for selling off the tube, being detailed in parliament later on Tuesday, is a key concern in the run up to national elections, due by May 22.

Pressure groups say the tube is crying out for more investment, with delays and station closures at their highest level for four years. Recent cuts to state spending on the system meant hundreds of repair projects had to be shelved.
Analysts say privatisation could raise as much as 2 billion pounds, but Labour said this would go into shareholders' pockets and no new investment would take place before 2001.
"Public control of the system is the only way to guarantee the future of services and fares," Shadow Transport Secretary Andrew Smith told Reuters.

"The Tory policy is 'run it down and sell it off', but we're in touch with financiers and construction companies interested in investment opportunites which could get the tube going without the delays, uncertainties and chaos.
Pointing to an enlarged tube map showing lines out to 40 peripheral stations axed, he said the sell off put at risk vital services.
In documents leaked to British newspapers at the weekend, Young said some uneconomic stations and services could be cut in the sell off.
A Labour spokesman said they estimated the Conservatives could lose five to ten parliamentary seats as a result of the privatisation plans.
